citation: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke rt-PA Stroke Study Group. Tissue plasminogen activator for acute ischemic stroke. N Engl J Med. 1995;333(24):1581-1587.
one_liner: IV alteplase within 3 hours of ischemic stroke onset improved 3-month functional outcomes (global OR 1.7, 95% CI 1.2–2.6) with increased symptomatic ICH (6.4% vs 0.6%) and no significant mortality difference.

pico.population: Adults with acute ischaemic stroke, measurable deficit on NIHSS, CT without intracranial haemorrhage, treatable within 3 hours of onset.
pico.intervention: IV alteplase (rt-PA) 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg), 10% bolus then infusion over 60 min; no antithrombotic agents for 24 h.
pico.comparison: Matching placebo with identical administration and co-intervention constraints.
pico.outcome: Part 2 primary: global test across four disability measures at 3 months (Barthel Index, mRS, GOS, NIHSS). Part 1 primary: early NIHSS improvement. Key secondaries: individual functional outcomes, symptomatic ICH, mortality.

background.existing_knowledge: Acute ischaemic stroke was a leading cause of death and disability with limited acute therapies. IV thrombolysis carried biological plausibility but feared intracranial haemorrhage trade-off.
background.knowledge_gap: No definitive trial had shown that IV alteplase within 3 hours improves functional outcomes.
background.hypothesis: IV alteplase within 3 hours improves early neurologic recovery and 3-month functional outcomes versus placebo, with acceptable safety.

methods.design: Randomised, multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial; stratified by centre and time to treatment (0–90 vs 91–180 min); two sequential parts with different primary endpoints.
methods.setting: Hospital-based acute stroke care with emergent CT, laboratory testing, and specialist evaluation.

inclusion: Acute ischaemic stroke with clearly defined time of onset
Measurable neurologic deficit on NIH Stroke Scale
exclusion: Stroke or serious head trauma in prior 3 months
GI or urinary tract haemorrhage within 21 days
Arterial puncture at noncompressible site within 7 days
Systolic BP >185 mmHg or diastolic BP >110 mmHg despite treatment
Anticoagulant use or heparin within 48 h with elevated aPTT

methods.intervention: IV alteplase (rt-PA) 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg), 10% bolus then infusion over 60 min; no antithrombotic agents for 24 h; BP maintained within prespecified limits.
methods.comparison: Matching placebo with identical administration and co-intervention constraints (no antithrombotics for 24 h, same BP targets).
methods.blinding: Double-blind; patients, clinicians, and outcome assessors blinded; CT scans interpreted centrally by a radiologist blinded to clinical data.
methods.sample_size_power: Part 2 planned 320 patients (160 per group) to detect a 20 percentage point difference with 95% power; total enrolled 624 across both parts.
methods.primary_outcome: Part 2: global test statistic across four 3-month disability measures (Barthel Index ≥95, mRS 0–1, GOS 1, NIHSS 0–1). Part 1: NIHSS improvement ≥4 or complete resolution at 24 hours.
secondary_outcomes: Individual components at 3 months (Barthel, mRS, GOS, NIHSS)
methods.follow_up: 3 months for functional outcomes; safety imaging at 24 h and 7–10 days.

headline_bullets: Alteplase improved 3-month disability outcomes across multiple scales (e.g., mRS 0–1 39% vs 26% in Part 2).
Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage within 36 h was higher with alteplase (6.4% vs 0.6%; p<0.001).
Mortality at 90 days was not significantly different (17% vs 21%; p=0.30).
Benefit observed in both early (0–90 min) and later (91–180 min) treatment strata (global OR 1.9 each).

outcomes_table.note: Global test across Barthel, mRS, GOS, NIHSS. Gatekeeping for individual components.

outcomes_table.outcome: Early neurologic improvement at 24 h (0–90 min stratum, combined)

safety: Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage within 36 h: 6.4% vs 0.6% (p<0.001). Part 1 6% vs 0%; Part 2 7% vs 1%.
Minor external bleeding within 10 days: 23% vs 3%.
New ischaemic stroke: Part 1 8% vs 7%; Part 2 4% vs 4% (similar).

domains.notes: Permuted-block randomisation (varying block sizes) stratified by centre and time-to-treatment (0–90 vs 91–180 min). Allocation concealment method not detailed, but blinding and identical placebo reduced selection risks.
Double-blind; certified examiners not involved in initial treatment assessed outcomes; CT scans interpreted centrally by a blinded radiologist.
Minimal missing data: Part 1 only 1 patient missing 3-month data; Part 2 7 of 1332 primary outcome measures missing, with prespecified handling (worst-score assignment). ITT analysis.
Dose delivery high: Part 1 full dose in 90% vs 92%; Part 2 93% vs 93%.

Stroke severity similar (median NIHSS 14 vs 14 in Part 1; 14 vs 15 in Part 2). Notable imbalances: weight in Part 1 (76±15 vs 80±18 kg), age in Part 2 (69±12 vs 66±13 years); covariate adjustment performed when variables differed at P<0.05.

internal_validity.verdict: Overall internal validity strong due to double-blinding, stratified randomisation, high protocol adherence, and minimal missing outcomes, though modest baseline imbalances and two-part design warrant attention.

domains.notes: Enrolled typical moderate-severity ischaemic strokes (median NIHSS 14–15), but restricted to patients treatable within 3h and excluded minor/rapidly improving strokes, recent bleeding risks, and severe hypertension.

Results apply best to health systems capable of rapid prehospital recognition, urgent CT, stroke expertise, and strict BP/coagulation management. Less generalisable where onset-to-needle >3h or infrastructure limited.

external_validity.verdict: External validity moderate: highly applicable to early-presenter patients in stroke-capable systems, but limited for later-presenting or excluded populations.

strengths: Clinically meaningful 3-month disability outcomes using multiple validated instruments
limitations: Two-part design with different primary endpoints
Modest sample size by modern standards
Early treatment window restricts applicability to rapid systems
Increased symptomatic ICH risk demands careful translation into practice

critical_appraisal.summary: The NINDS trial provides high-quality evidence that alteplase within 3 hours improves disability outcomes, with acceptable but clearly increased ICH risk, and drove system-level transformation of acute stroke care.
strengths: Clinically meaningful 3-month disability outcomes using multiple validated instruments
weaknesses: Two-part design with different primary endpoints
Modest sample size by modern standards
Early treatment window restricts applicability to rapid systems
Increased symptomatic ICH risk demands careful translation into practice

sections.authors_conclusion: IV alteplase within 3 hours of acute ischaemic stroke onset improves 3-month functional outcomes, with increased symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage but no significant mortality difference.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: This trial changed practice by establishing a time-dependent benefit of alteplase and creating the modern emergency stroke pathway.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Patients meeting trial inclusion/exclusion criteria, treated within 3 hours in a stroke-capable centre.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: It does not imply safety beyond 3 hours without advanced imaging selection, nor that thrombolysis replaces endovascular therapy for large vessel occlusion.
implementation_caveats: Strict BP control and 24h avoidance of antithrombotics required
Informed consent and monitoring for ICH
Optimise door-to-needle times to maximise benefit

controversies.notes: Accompanying editorial emphasized that thrombolysis crossed a clinical threshold but required system-level readiness and careful patient selection.
Some questioned whether chance baseline imbalances inflated benefit; a formal reanalysis confirmed the primary result was robust to imbalance.
Subsequent pooled and individual-patient meta-analyses reinforced a strong time-dependent benefit, contextualising the 3-hour window as high-yield.
Real-world studies showed thrombolysis can be delivered with acceptable haemorrhage rates, but frequent protocol deviations highlighted need for governance, audit, and time targets.
Contemporary guidelines now recommend IV alteplase within 3 hours, with extended windows for selected patients.

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: IV alteplase within 3 hours of ischemic stroke improves 3-month disability outcomes with an acceptable ICH risk increase, no mortality penalty.
